name: Sotho
confidence_why: Jacottet 1906, Tucker 1929, Doke & Mofokeng 1957 (as quoted by Kunene 1961), Nussbaum & Lijane 1968 and the instrumental study of Mixdorff et al. 2011 all put the prominent syllable on the penult of a statement or isolated word, but Kunene 1961, a native speaker's phonology dissertation, denies that Southern Sotho is a stress language at all, treats the penultimate length as a phrase-level statement marker and places inherent main stress on the root syllable, so the penultimate reading is the clear majority view but not uncontested.
catalog_quote: This length is never found on the penultimate syllable of any word when it occurs in the middle of a sentence.

new_statements.quote: Sesotho, like many other languages of Africa, is a tone language. A tone language is one that makes a particular use of pitch as an element of speech. [...] we will use only two tonemes which contrast with each other. They are high (H) and low (L) tone. [...] Any syllable in any given word is pronounced with its appropriate high or low toneme. [p. 11] [...] Sesotho does not have long and short sounds. [...] Sesotho, like many other Southern African languages, uses what Cole calls penultimate length. Penultimate length refers to the lengthening of the syllable before the last one in polysyllabic words: Examples: ba:na, [tsamaea], nta:te, [...]. Furthermore, there is prolonged length which occurs in emotional or dramatic speech. This kind of length can be both ultimate and penultimate [p. 12]
new_statements.citation: Corps, USA / Peace (1996). Language manual II : Sesotho. Peace Corps (Lesotho).
new_statements.locator: Chapter II 'Tone and Length', printed pp. 11-12 = PDF pages 15-16 of the ERIC scan ED401739
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened, PDF pages 15-16 (printed pp. 11-12, Chapter II 'Tone and Length'). Every sentence of the quote is present in order: 'Sesotho, like many other languages of Africa, is a tone language. A tone language is one that makes a particular use of pitch as an element of speech.'.. 'we will use only two tonemes which contrast with each other. They are high (H) and low (L) tone.'.. 'Any syllable in any given word is pronounced with its appropriate high or low toneme.' (p. 15) and 'Sesotho does not have long and short sounds.' (page break) 'Sesotho, like many other Southern African languages, uses what Cole calls penultimate length. Penultimate length refers to the lengthening of the syllable bef…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed-penultimate record: the manual locates the language's word-level prominence (realised as length) on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words, which is the usual basis for the penultimate-stress reading in Southern Bantu; it adds that the language is a H/L tone language and that the prominence is a length phenomenon, but it never calls it stress and gives no statement on stress as such.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The manual never uses the word 'stress'. It states that Sesotho is a two-toneme (H/L) tone language and that, instead of contrastive vowel length, it has 'penultimate length': the syllable before the last in a polysyllabic word is lengthened (ba:na, nta:te). Prolonged length in emotional/dramatic speech may fall on the final or penultimate syllable, with idiolectal variation.
new_statements.exceptions: Prolonged (expressive) length can be ultimate or penultimate in emotional or dramatic speech (Thaba e:tla vs Thaba ela:; Oa e:ta / Oa e::ta / Oa eta::); the difference is called idiolectal.
new_statements.identity_note: Peace Corps 1996 is a Lesotho training manual, i.e. Sesotho (Southern Sotho) as spoken in Lesotho; it cites Guma 1971 and Cole for the tone and length statements. Clements 1991 treats Sesotho (Southern Sotho) with a consultant from Motsethabong, Welkom, South Africa, and states that Tswana and Northern Sotho have nearly identical vowel systems; no dialect-specific prosody claims.

tone_statements.citation: Wissing, Daan & Justus C. Roux. 2017. The Status of Tone in Sesotho: A Production and Perception Study. Nordic Journal of African Studies 26(4): 384-402.
tone_statements.quote: It is generally maintained that the Sotho languages (i.e. Sesotho sa Leboa, Setswana and Sesotho) are tone languages (Tucker 1929; Doke and Mofokeng 1957; Guma 1971; Roux 1983; Krüger and Snyman 1988; Poulos and Louwrens 1994). As in many Bantu languages, the tone system of the Sotho family underlyingly has a two-way contrast (L, H) (Doke 1954; Cole 1955; Zerbian 2006). [...] As a tonal language, Sesotho uses pitch variations to convey lexical or grammatical meaning. Doke and Mofokeng (1957) provide the following Sesotho examples of minimal pairs in isolation: ho báká (‘to repent’) vs. ho baka (‘to cause’); ho téná (‘to put on’) vs. ho tena (‘to disgust’)
tone_statements.locator: pp. 384-385, section 1 Introduction; conclusion on p. 397: 'in the mouths and ears of these participants, tone is not alive and well in Sesotho'

tone_statements.citation: Mohasi, Lehlohonolo. 2015. Prosody modelling for a Sesotho text-to-speech system using the Fujisaki model. PhD dissertation, Stellenbosch University. 126 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Sesotho is a grammatical tone language and like most Bantu languages, it uses a register tone system where the distinguishing feature is the relative difference between a high and a low pitch, also denoted as high tone (H) and low tone (L). … In Sesotho, there are two types of high tones: lexical high tones and grammatical high tones. Lexical high tones assimilate by spreading one syllable to the right whereas grammatical high tones spread all the way to the end of the verb. Dissimilatory processes, on the other hand, involve various kinds of high tone deletion and delinking.
tone_statements.summary: Register tone system with two tones, high and low, carried by the syllable; lexical high spreads one syllable right, grammatical high to the end of the verb; downstep between and within phrases.

tone_statements.citation: Mohasi, Lehlohonolo, Thomas Niesler & Hansjörg Mixdorff. 2014. Perceptual evaluation of the effect of mismatched Fujisaki model commands and surface tone in Sesotho. In Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2014 (Dublin), 582-586. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2014-105
tone_statements.quote: Sesotho uses a register tone system with two tones, high and low. The Fujisaki model and surface tonal transcription have shown a strong agreement on the interpretation of tone in Sesotho sentences [10]. … Tone sandhi … is present in Sesotho as pointed out by Demuth [11], and is modelled by the surface tonal rules HTD (spreading of a lexical high tone to the immediate right syllable) and IHTS (iterative spreading of a high tone to the end of a verb).
tone_statements.summary: Register tone system with two level tones, high and low; lexical high tones spread rightward by sandhi rules; each syllable surfaces as H or L; downstep mentioned but not analysed; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Wissing, Daan P. 2012. On the many faces of tone in Southern Sotho: a case study. In H. S. Ndinga-Koumba-Binza & S. E. Bosch (eds.), Language Science and Language Technology in Africa: Festschrift for Justus C. Roux, 47-60. Stellenbosch: SUN MeDIA.
tone_statements.quote: For example, in the case of Southern Sotho tone is said to distinguish grammatical and lexical meaning in all of the languages of the Sotho-Tswana group. While low tones can exist next to each other, high tones cannot (but see reference to Doke and Mofokeng’s 1957 description further down below). … According to Doke and Mofokeng’s (1957:46; 48; 302) description ke has a low tone in the present tense (positive), but is high in the negative. As maintained by these authors, such description applies to all speakers. I will put to the test this description
tone_statements.locator: p. 48, sec. 2 'Basic outline of tone and vowel quality in Sesotho'; conclusion p. 57
tone_statements.summary: High and low tones distinguishing lexical and grammatical meaning (after Doke & Mofokeng 1957); F0 data find the low/high contrast on ke robust only for adult males, suggesting partial loss.

tone_statements.citation: Raborife, Mpho. 2011 [issued 2012]. Tone labelling algorithm for Sesotho. MSc dissertation, Faculty of Science, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg.
tone_statements.quote: Sesotho is a tonal language; it uses pitch variations to convey grammatical or lexical meaning. … Sesotho has only two tonal levels, namely the high tone (H) and the low tone (L) … Sesotho is classified as a grammatical tone language with a restricted tonal system, that is, a system where not every syllable must be encoded for tone in the lexicon [Demuth 1995]. … In sum, it is only the high tones that are explicitly specified on the syllables in the speaker’s mental lexicon, and low tones appear when a syllable is tonally under-specified.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.2 'The Tonal System of Sesotho', pp. 7-8
tone_statements.summary: Two tone levels, high and low; only high tones are lexically specified, low is filled in by default; syllables (incl. syllabic nasals) bear tone; H spreads and delinks by rule within prosodic domains.

tone_statements.citation: Letele, Gladstone Llewellyn (1950/51). The role of tone in the Southern Sotho language. Univ. of London.
tone_statements.quote: In order to describe the tonal features or the SS sentence three tone levels have to be recognised, namely low level, high level and mid level. … The mid tone, as an Essential Tone,'* onxy occurs after a high tone. In all other positions the occurrence of a tone at mid level is usually a speech reaxisation of what is essentially a low or high tone* TONE PATTERNS: All woras, phrases and sentences of S3 are … characterised by Tone Patterns. That is to say, each syllable of a word has tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 6, sections 'TONE LEVELS' and 'TONE PATTERNS' (down-step/up-step: pp. 10, 11, 14)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Three tone levels, low, high and mid, with mid contrastive only after a high; each syllable carries a tone; glides only on long syllables; down-step and up-step key changes mark word junctions.

tone_statements.citation: Tucker, A. N. 1949. Sotho-Nguni orthography and tone-marking. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 13(1): 200-224.
tone_statements.quote: There are three main static levels of tone in Sotho—high level, mid level, and low level. … The last tone is only to be found on the final syllable of a sentence, and is a dependent form of the “ not-high ” toneme. … There are also three dynamic tones, found mostly in the penultimate syllable … There are thus three tonemes1 in Sotho, whose scope may be recapitulated •as follows:— ■la {High) Falling Toneme, found in ideophones and also on the penultimate syllable of a sentence … ’la High Toneme, with the following members … la Mid {or “ not high ”) Toneme, with the following members
tone_statements.locator: pp. 214-215, Part III 'Intonation', 'Sotho Basic Tones' = (fn. 1 p. 215: Jones's two-toneme count; step down pp. 221-222)
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes: high-falling, high and mid ('not high'), each with positional variants (low level only sentence-final); four inherent word tone patterns; automatic step-down between words.

audit.recode_to: Keep kind = fixed penult (penultimate prominence is what Jacottet 1906, Tucker 1929, Doke & Mofokeng 1957 §60 [via Kunene], Nussbaum & Lijane 1968 and Mixdorff et al. 2011 all describe), but (a) reclassify domain not stated by the source -> phrase/utterance: Tucker §250, Kunene §3.4 and Nussbaum & Lijane cycle 4 all state the penult lengthening sits on the penult of the statement/pause group (and of words in isolation), is absent on word-penults mid-sentence and is suppressed in questions; (b) add a caution: Kunene 1961 (UCT PhD, pp.153-167) holds that 'S.Sotho is not a stress language', that penult prominence is LENGTH, and that inherent word stress is on the root (stem-initial) syllable with only secondary stress on the penult in stems of 4+ syllables — an explicit challenge to Doke's penult-stress statement; (c) note that Jacottet's 'last syllable when it ends in ng' clause is penult-regular once final ŋ is counted as a syllabic nasal (cf. Kunene sefate:ng, Nussbaum ha-n-tle); (d) when a copy of Doke & Mofokeng 1957 is obtained, make §60 the deciding citation.
audit.reasoning: Quote check: Jacottet 1906:4 confirmed verbatim on the page scan we hold; Tucker 1929:99-100 confirmed verbatim in the copy downloaded now. The classification rests on a 1906 missionary teaching course plus a 1929 comparative-phonetics monograph whose examples are Tswana; Glottolog lists a 491-pp reference grammar (Doke & Mofokeng 1957, not open, not yet obtained) and a 497-pp phonology PhD (Kunene 1961, downloaded now). Every source opened agrees the penult of a statement/isolation form is long/prominent, so the penult coding itself is not in danger, but (1) three opened sources say the phenomenon is utterance/phrase-level, so domain should not stay not stated by the source, and (2) Kunene 1961 explicitly disputes penult word stress (root-syllable inherent stress; penult = phrasal length), which the record does not mention. Hence 'thin' (old pedagogical deciding source, better sources exist, one of them dissenting on

sources.quote: 'The penultimate (second to last) syllable of a statement is longer than other syllables. You can observe this lengthening on the /n/ in hantle and on the first /e/ in khotso ... This lengthening is automatic in statements, but ... it does not occur with questions. It also occurs when words or names are spoken in isolation: Thabo [aa], lebitso [ii].' Questions are marked 'by a raising of the entire pitch level ... and by an absence of penultimate lengthening'. (Syllabic nasal counts as the penult in ha.n.tle.)

sources.quote: Length §3.4: penult of a word/phrase/clause uttered non-interrogatively (or before pause+downstep) is long; short in questions; 'Length of the penult is thus the sole criterion for distinction between questions and statements' (examples incl. isolation words: Maso:pha, sefate:ng, waha:e). Stress p.153: 'S.Sotho is not a stress language. Strong stresses in this language are not easy to perceive in speech that is not extra-normally emphatic.' §3.43: quotes Doke & Mofokeng §60 'main stress is typically on the penultimate syllable' and Tucker §252, then: 'both Tucker's and Doke-and-Mofokeng's conc
sources.note: Only full phonetic monograph on S. Sotho length and stress; separates phrase-penult LENGTH (statements/isolation, absent in questions) from inherent word STRESS, which it places on the root syllable, explicitly challenging Doke's penult stress — must be registered as a caution/dissent on this record.

sources.citation: Mixdorff, H., Mohasi, L., Machobane, M. & Niesler, T. 2011. A study on the perception of tone and intonation in Sesotho. Proc. Interspeech 2011, Florence. doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2011-796
sources.quote: Questions show 'a conspicuous shortening of the penultimate syllable which is the carrier of word stress in Sesotho'; perception test: shortening the penult to 70% is the strongest cue turning a statement into a question (instrumental, resynthesis-based).
sources.note: Modern instrumental support that the (utterance-)penult is the locus of prominence ('carrier of word stress') and that its lengthening is suspended in questions — upgrades strength of the evidence beyond 1906/1929 impressionistic sources.

sources.citation: Tucker, A. N. 1929. The comparative phonetics of the Suto-Chuana group of Bantu languages. London: Longmans, Green & Co. (archive.org item comparativephone0000tuck)
sources.quote: §250: 'In a normal statement, the penultimate syllable, whether a word in itself or part of a word, is pronounced long. ... This length is never found on the penultimate syllable of any word when it occurs in the middle of a sentence.' §251: in questions/commands the penult is not lengthened. §252: 'In a normal sentence, the last two syllables are both stressed ... the stress on the final syllable is subjective, while that on the penultimate syllable is primarily objective.' Examples 'from SeChuana'.
sources.note: Cited in the record as corroboration and as the domain quotation (the domain locator) but was not yet obtained; now obtained by the project so the §250-252 quotes are verifiable (confirmed).

sources.citation: Zeller, Jochen (2004). Relative clause formation in the Bantu languages of South Africa. Southern African linguistics and applied language studies 22. pp. 75-93.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: A syntax paper on relative-clause formation (relative markers, relative concords, grammaticalisation). No statement about word stress, accent or tone in any language; the only prosody-related string is the reference list entry 'Harford & Demuth 1999. Prosody outranks syntax..'. Circumflexes in the Sotho examples (yô, dikgômo, fâle, golô) are standard orthography, not tone marks, and the text never comments on them. sources.quote: Sesotho uses a register tone system with two tones, high and low. The Fujisaki model and surface tonal transcription have shown a strong agreement on the interpretation of tone in Sesotho sentences [10]. … Tone sandhi … is present in Sesotho as pointed out by Demuth [11], and is modelled by the surface tonal rules HTD (spreading of a lexical high tone to the immediate right syllable) and IHTS (iterative spreading of a high tone to the end of a verb).

sources.quote: Sesotho is a tonal language; it uses pitch variations to convey grammatical or lexical meaning. … Sesotho has only two tonal levels, namely the high tone (H) and the low tone (L) … Sesotho is classified as a grammatical tone language with a restricted tonal system, that is, a system where not every syllable must be encoded for tone in the lexicon [Demuth 1995]. … In sum, it is only the high tones that are explicitly specified on the syllables in the speaker’s mental lexicon, and low tones appear when a syllable is tonally under-specified.
sources.locator: sec. 2.2 'The Tonal System of Sesotho', pp. 7-8
sources.note: Two tone levels, high and low; only high tones are lexically specified, low is filled in by default; syllables (incl. syllabic nasals) bear tone; H spreads and delinks by rule within prosodic domains.

tone.quote: In order to describe the tonal features or the SS sentence three tone levels have to be recognised, namely low level, high level and mid level. … The mid tone, as an Essential Tone,'* onxy occurs after a high tone. In all other positions the occurrence of a tone at mid level is usually a speech reaxisation of what is essentially a low or high tone* TONE PATTERNS: All woras, phrases and sentences of S3 are … characterised by Tone Patterns. That is to say, each syllable of a word has tone.
tone.locator: p. 6, sections 'TONE LEVELS' and 'TONE PATTERNS' (down-step/up-step: pp. 10, 11, 14)

tone.summary: Three tone levels, low, high and mid, with mid contrastive only after a high; each syllable carries a tone; glides only on long syllables; down-step and up-step key changes mark word junctions.
